questions.question: What does a group homomorphism preserve?
options: The group operation across a map between groups
The printed order of elements in a table
The exact numeric encoding of every element
The fact that every codomain element is used
questions.explanation: A homomorphism satisfies f(a*b) = f(a) * f(b), using the domain operation on the left and codomain operation on the right.

questions.question: What is an isomorphism between two groups?
options: A structure-preserving bijection with a structure-preserving inverse
Any function whose output values are smaller than its input values
A subgroup that contains only the identity element
A map that turns every element into the codomain identity
questions.explanation: An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism. It means the two groups have the same structure under different labels.

questions.question: For additive groups, which equation says that f is a homomorphism?
options: f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)
f(a + b) = f(a) * f(b)
f(a) = a for every possible input
f(a) is always larger than f(b)
questions.explanation: For additive groups, preserving the operation means the image of a sum equals the sum of the images.

questions.question: In the map Z/12Z -> Z/4Z given by f(x) = x mod 4, what is the kernel?
options: {0, 4, 8}, the elements that map to 0 in Z/4Z
{0, 1, 2, 3}, the first four elements of Z/12Z
{4, 5, 6, 7}, the middle coset of Z/12Z
{1, 5, 9}, the elements congruent to 1 modulo 4
questions.explanation: The kernel is the preimage of the codomain identity. Here the codomain identity is 0, so the kernel is {0, 4, 8}.

questions.question: What does the image of a homomorphism contain?
options: All codomain elements that are actually hit by the map
All domain elements that map to the identity
Only elements that fail the operation-preservation test
Only elements whose numeric encodings are prime
questions.explanation: The image is the set of outputs f(x) as x ranges over the domain.

questions.question: Why is k -> g^k a useful homomorphism in a cyclic group generated by g?
options: It turns addition of exponents into multiplication of group elements
It removes the need for an identity element in the target group
It proves discrete logarithms are easy in every large group
It maps every exponent to a value outside the generated subgroup
questions.explanation: The rule g^(a+b) = g^a * g^b means the exponent map preserves the operation from additive exponents to multiplicative group elements.

questions.question: What security mistake can happen when a protocol confuses a homomorphism with an isomorphism?
options: It may assume secrets are uniquely represented when the kernel collapses several inputs
It may require one extra byte for every serialized public key
It may make the group operation non-associative in the implementation
It may prevent the identity from being represented in the codomain
questions.explanation: A nontrivial kernel means distinct domain elements map to the same output. Treating such a map as one-to-one can break reasoning about secrets.

questions.question: For a finite homomorphism, what size relation should kernel and image satisfy?
options: |domain| = |kernel| * |image|
|codomain| = |kernel| * |domain|
|kernel| = |domain| * |codomain|
|image| is always larger than |domain|
questions.explanation: The finite first isomorphism theorem implies that the domain splits into equal-size fibers over the image, so |domain| = |kernel| * |image|.
